solution:
**The band picture.** In an isolated atom the electrons occupy discrete energy levels. When a solid forms, a very large number of atoms are packed close together (about 2 to 3 A apart), the outermost electrons of neighbouring atoms interact, and each level must split into a great many sub-levels so that Pauli's exclusion principle is not violated — any one level can hold only two electrons, one spin up and one spin down. The sub-levels lie so close together that they form a practically continuous ENERGY BAND.

The topmost occupied band is the **valence band**. The next band above it, which valence electrons can be raised into, is the **conduction band**. The separation between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band is the **energy gap** or **band gap**. Only electrons that can reach the conduction band are free to carry current, so the width of this gap decides the electrical behaviour of the solid. Solids are classified into three types on this basis.

| Type of solid | Band structure | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Conductor (metal) | Valence band and conduction band OVERLAP; there is no band gap | Electrons gain energy from even a small applied field very easily and are readily available for conduction, so the conductivity is very high |
| Semiconductor | A band gap exists but is fairly small, of the order of one electron volt or less (Si 1.12 eV, Ge 0.66 eV at 300 K) | At absolute zero all levels are filled and it cannot conduct; at room temperature thermal energy of order \(kT\) lifts a few electrons across the gap, each leaving a hole behind, so conductivity is intermediate and rises with temperature |
| Insulator | A WIDE gap between valence and conduction band (diamond, about 5.47 eV) | Electrons find it very difficult to gain enough energy to reach the conduction band, so almost no carriers are available and the conductivity is extremely low |

The ordering matches the measured conductivities in Table 14.1: silver \(6.30 \times 10^{7}\), silicon \(1.56 \times 10^{-3}\) and glass \(10^{-11}\) to \(10^{-15}\) S m\(^{-1}\).

[Note: the chapter warns that this band structure describes the ENERGY of electrons in the solid and does not represent the physical structure of the solid in any way.]

An **intrinsic** semiconductor is a pure semiconductor, such as pure silicon or pure germanium. An **extrinsic** semiconductor is one to which a small amount of a suitable impurity has been deliberately added; the process of adding the impurity is called **doping**, the impurity is the **dopant** and the parent atoms are the **hosts**.

| Point of difference | Intrinsic semiconductor | Extrinsic semiconductor |
|---|---|---|
| Composition | Pure; no impurity added | Doped with a controlled amount of impurity |
| Origin of carriers | Only thermal breaking of covalent bonds | Thermal breaking plus the carriers supplied by the dopant atoms |
| Carrier densities | Equal: \(n_{e} = n_{h}\) | Unequal: \(n_{e} \gg n_{h}\) for n-type, \(n_{h} \gg n_{e}\) for p-type |
| Majority and minority carriers | No distinction — both carriers are equally numerous | n-type: electrons majority, holes minority. p-type: holes majority, electrons minority |
| Conductivity at room temperature | Very low, which is why no electronic device can be fabricated from it | Appreciably higher; extrinsic semiconductors are far better conductors than intrinsic ones |
| Control | Fixed by the material and its temperature alone | Can be controlled by controlling the amount of impurity added, expressed in parts per million (ppm) |
| Types | Only one | Two — n-type (pentavalent dopant such as P, As, Sb) and p-type (trivalent dopant such as B, Al, In) |

**What is the same in both:** the product of the two carrier densities, \(n_{e} \cdot n_{h} = n_{i}^{2}\), holds for a semiconductor either way; and BOTH kinds of crystal are electrically NEUTRAL as a whole. In an n-type crystal the extra electrons are supplied by donor atoms that are themselves left positively charged, and in a p-type crystal the acceptor atoms become negatively charged, so no net charge appears in either case.

**How the region forms.** When p-type and n-type material are joined, the large density gradient across the junction makes electrons diffuse from the n-side into the p-side, where they fill holes and produce negative acceptor ions, while holes effectively migrate into the n-region leaving positive donor ions behind. The accumulation of these opposite charges on the two sides builds a potential difference across the junction — the **potential barrier** — about 0.6 to 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 to 0.35 V for germanium. Free carriers cannot exist where there is a potential barrier, so the region on either side of the junction is left completely devoid of charge carriers. That region is the **depletion layer** or **depletion region**.

**Why it matters.**

1. **It stops the diffusion and creates equilibrium.** The barrier prevents the continuous diffusion of carriers across the junction, so a state of electrostatic equilibrium is reached. Without it the two materials would simply mix their carriers until nothing distinguished them. The barrier exists even when the device is connected to no external source at all.

2. **It is the seat of the junction's electric field.** Because the n-side is left positive with respect to the p-side, an electric field exists across the region, directed from the n-side to the p-side.

3. **Its width can be CONTROLLED by an external voltage, and this is the useful property.** Forward bias opposes the built-in potential, so the barrier and the depletion width DECREASE and the junction offers a low resistance path, passing a current of a few milliamperes. Reverse bias adds to the built-in potential, so the barrier and the depletion width INCREASE and the junction behaves like a high resistance, passing only a leakage current of a few microamperes.

4. **This asymmetry is what makes a diode a diode.** Because the same device conducts easily one way and blocks the other, it acts as a one way switch or gate — closed in forward bias, open in reverse bias. The chapter notes that the p-n junction is on this account the basis of almost all modern electronic devices, and the p-n junction diode is the basic block of a number of semiconductor devices.

**Features of the depletion region, as listed in the chapter:** it is formed by diffusion of electrons from the n-region to the p-region, leaving positively charged ions in the n-region; the p-region accumulates negative charges and the n-region positive charges; the accumulation on either side forms the potential barrier and prevents flow of charges across it; there are no charges in this region; and the region has a higher potential on the n-side and a lower potential on the p-side.

**The arrangement.** The diode is forward biased: the positive terminal of the external supply is connected to the anode (the p-side) and the negative terminal to the cathode (the n-side). The graph is drawn with the forward voltage \(V\) along the x-axis and the forward current \(I\), in milliamperes, along the y-axis.

**Shape of the curve.**

1. **Below the knee.** For small applied voltages the current is very low. The applied voltage has not yet cancelled enough of the built-in potential barrier, so few carriers can cross the junction and the curve rises only very gradually, running almost along the voltage axis.

2. **The knee.** At a certain voltage the current suddenly begins to rise sharply. That point on the curve is called the **knee point** and the corresponding voltage the **knee voltage**. The chapter gives it as about 0.7 V for a silicon diode and about 0.3 V for a germanium diode.

3. **Above the knee.** Once the applied voltage exceeds the knee voltage the barrier is largely overcome, the depletion region has narrowed and the junction presents a low resistance path, so the current rises very steeply for a very small further increase in voltage. The curve becomes nearly vertical: the diode effectively behaves as a short circuit and can conduct a very large current.

**Consequences.**

- The characteristic is markedly NON-linear, so the diode does not obey Ohm's law and a single value of resistance will not describe it. Two resistances are therefore defined from this curve: the static or DC resistance \(R_{g} = \dfrac{V}{I}\), the ratio of the DC voltage across the diode to the DC current through it at a particular voltage; and the dynamic or AC resistance \(r_{g} = \dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}\), which is the reciprocal of the slope of the characteristic at the operating point and therefore depends on which point is chosen.
- Because the diode becomes practically a short circuit above the knee, a resistor must be connected in SERIES with it to limit the current. If the current exceeds the specified value the diode heats up through Joule heating and can be physically damaged.

[Note: for an IDEAL diode the curve degenerates to a vertical line along the current axis — zero resistance in forward bias, as in Fig. 14.27.]

The depletion region is bounded by the potential barrier, so anything the external voltage does to that barrier it also does to the width of the region. There are three cases.

**1. Zero bias — no external voltage.** The barrier set up by the diffusion of carriers exists on its own; the chapter notes it is present even when the device is connected to no external power source. The depletion region has its natural equilibrium width. Majority carriers cannot cross, though a few minority carriers drift both ways so that the net current is zero — a state of dynamic equilibrium.

**2. Forward bias — the width DECREASES.** The positive terminal is connected to the p-side and the negative terminal to the n-side, so the applied voltage OPPOSES the built-in potential of the junction. The barrier is thus reduced. At the same time electrons in the n-region and holes in the p-region are pushed TOWARDS the junction, so charge carriers move into the region that was depleted and it narrows. The chapter states plainly that the width of the depletion layer decreases with an increase in the applied forward voltage. A narrower region means a low resistance path and a large forward current, of the order of a few milliamperes.

**3. Reverse bias — the width INCREASES.** The positive terminal is connected to the n-side and the negative terminal to the p-side, so the applied voltage ADDS to the built-in potential. The barrier is thus increased. Electrons in the n-region and holes in the p-region are now pulled AWAY from the junction, leaving a still wider layer stripped of carriers, so the depletion region broadens. The chapter states that its width increases when a reverse voltage is applied, and increases further as that voltage is raised. A wider region means a high resistance, and only a small leakage current of a few microamperes flows.

**Summary.**

| External voltage | Effect on potential barrier | Effect on depletion width | Resulting current |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zero bias | Built-in barrier only | Equilibrium width | Net current zero |
| Forward bias | Reduced | Decreases | Large, a few mA |
| Reverse bias | Increased | Increases | Very small leakage, a few \(\mu\)A |

Because reversing the polarity changes the width of the depletion layer in opposite directions, the current through the diode is asymmetrical — which is exactly what allows a p-n junction to be used as a one way switch.

[Note: if the reverse voltage is raised far enough the junction overheats, covalent bonds break, a large number of carriers become available and the reverse current rises abruptly. This is the breakdown of the junction and the diode no longer behaves like a diode.]
